o: We must convert an integer (possibly negative) into its base-7 string. The standard technique is repeated division: repeatedly take `num % 7` to get the next least-significant digit, then integer-divide by 7, until the number becomes 0. Digits come out in reverse order, so we prepend or reverse at the end. For **num = 100**: 100 % 7 = 2, 100/7 = 14; 14 % 7 = 0, 14/7 = 2; 2 % 7 = 2, 2/7 = 0 → digits collected [2,0,2] reversed give "202". For **num = -7**: work with |num| = 7: 7 % 7 = 0, 7/7 = 1; 1 % 7 = 1 → digits [0,1], prepend '-' → "-10". Constraints of ±10^7 mean at most ~9 base-7 digits, so any linear-in-digits approach is trivially fast. Edge cases: num = 0 must return "0" (the loop body never runs otherwise), and negatives only need a sign prefix since we convert the absolute value.
k: Repeatedly taking num % 7 yields base-7 digits from least significant to most significant.
Handle num = 0 explicitly and convert abs(num), prefixing '-' for negatives.
The result has at most O(log₇ n) ≈ 9 digits for n ≤ 10^7.

a.n: Approach 1: Repeated Division with String Building
a.i: Convert the absolute value by peeling off one digit per iteration using modulo and division. Since digits emerge least-significant first, build them into a list and reverse at the end (or prepend). This works because a number in base b satisfies n = d_k·b^k + ... + d_0, and n mod b always extracts d_0.
s: Record whether num is negative and set n = abs(num).
While n > 0: append str(n % 7) to a list, then n //= 7.
Reverse the digit list, join into a string.
Prefix "-" if the original number was negative.
a.t: O(log₇ n) — each iteration divides n by 7, giving about log₇(10^7) ≈ 9 iterations.
a.sp: O(log₇ n) — storage for the digit list/string.

a.i: Most languages offer built-ins that handle this directly: Python's format/int-to-string tricks, Java's Integer.toString(num, 7), or C++'s std::to_chars-style manual loop. Alternatively, recursion naturally builds digits most-significant-first: f(n) = f(n/7) + digit(n%7). These are one-liners worth knowing in interviews but hide the mechanics.
s: Use the language's built-in base conversion (e.g., Java's Integer.toString(num, 7)).
In Python, use numpy.base_repr or a recursive helper: if n < 7 return sign+str(n), else recurse on n//7 and append n%7.
a.t: O(log₇ n) — same digit count as Approach 1; built-ins do the identical division loop internally.
a.sp: O(log₇ n) — output string plus recursion stack (recursive variant).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 — it demonstrates you understand positional numeral systems, which is what the interviewer wants to see; mention built-ins (Approach 2) as a follow-up aside. Pitfalls: forgetting num = 0 (infinite/empty output), mishandling negatives (convert abs value, then prefix '-'), and in C++ beware INT_MIN whose absolute value overflows int — use long long. Follow-ups often generalize to arbitrary bases (LeetCode 168/171 Excel columns, base -2 in LeetCode 1017) or ask to convert back from base 7 to decimal.
